newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian prime minister to hand in resignation.
newsitem.headline: Latvian prime minister to hand in resignation.

text.p: Reformist Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele, his administration shaken by corruption scandals, bowed to pressure from the parties which form his government on Friday and said he would resign.
"I will on Monday hand in to the president an announcement about the end of the powers of my government," Shkele told a news conference.
Shkele, a tough, non-party businessman, has been undermined in recent weeks by the resignation of a string of ministers amid corruption scandals.
Relations between Shkele and the seven ruling parties have also been deteriorating amid increasing bitterness. It is not clear who will replace him.
Shkele, who came to power at the end of 1995, has been credited with giving a big boost to the reforms which Latvia launched after it quit the former Soviet Union in 1991.
The prime minister presented a plan this week to save the government but this had been rejected by the ruling parties.
"I was told that it had been a mistake to place a (politically) unaffiliated person at the head of the government and I was accused of destroying party democracy," Shkele added.
Shkele's government has been fragile from the start, given the rainbow nature of the coalition, which includes parties from the nationalist right to moderate centrists and leftists.
Shkele has gone through several crises, most notably in January when he resigned in fury after President Guntis Ulmanis urged parliament to reject a proposed new finance minister.
The two leaders settled their differences and a new Shkele government was backed by parliament in February.
His latest troubles came when four ministers were forced to quit after they were found to have violated anti-corruption laws by holding state and private jobs at the same time.
A fifth, Interior Minister Dainis Turlais, handed in his resignation after the death of eight children at a firefighting show when the rescue basket they were in plunged to the ground.
Shkele has several times attacked the parties which form his government, accusing them of working only for their immediate interests.
Despite his troubles, Shkele had enough support to push on with reforms and restore confidence in an economy hit in 1995 by the collapse amid scandal of its largest bank, Banka Baltiya.
Shkele restored a sense of financial discipline by pushing through balanced budgets in 1996 and 1997 and planning deficit-free packages for 1998/1999.
He has also given a big push to privatisation, which seemed to have stagnated under the previous administration.
"I hope that the work succesfully begun, especially in getting the basic things in order, will be thoroughly continued by the parties, and the economy will be strengthened," he said.
